topics.title: Tu or Lei? How formal to be in Italy
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about how people address each other in Italy. This is habit, not law: it varies by region, age, workplace and person, so listen to how others speak.
topics.intro: Italian has two main ways to say you to one person: tu and Lei. Tu is the usual choice with friends, family, colleagues and young people, and Lei shows respect to older strangers or in formal situations.
topics.question: Esiste una forma di cortesia nella tua lingua? (Does your language have a formal way to say you?)
facts: Use tu with friends, family, children and people of your own age.
Use Lei with older people you do not know, and in formal situations: a doctor, an office, a bank. Lei is often written with a capital L, so it is not confused with lei (she).
The verb changes: with tu you say Come stai? and with Lei you say Come sta? Lei is used for men and for women.
In many workplaces, especially with young colleagues, people use tu even with the boss. Listen to what the others say.
For a group, say voi. In some parts of the south, older people also use voi as a polite you for one person. It sounds old-fashioned to many ears, but it is not wrong.
Titles often go with Lei: dottore or dottoressa (for anyone with a degree, not only doctors), professore or professoressa, signora, signore.
Not sure? Start with Lei and wait. Often the other person says: Ci diamo del tu? (Shall we use tu?) or Dammi pure del tu (Feel free to use tu with me).

topics.title: Greetings: baci, handshake, Ciao and Buongiorno
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about greetings in Italy. This is habit, not law: it varies by region, age, situation and person. Follow what the other person does.
topics.intro: In Italy people greet with a word first, and often with a touch: two kisses on the cheeks (due baci) or a handshake. What is usual depends on the region, the age and the situation.
topics.question: Come saluti nel tuo paese? (How do you greet people in your country?)
facts: Due baci: you touch cheeks, one side and then the other, and the kiss is mostly in the air. It is common between friends and relatives, and between a woman and a man who know each other.
Between men, a handshake is most common. Relatives and close friends may hug or kiss on the cheeks.
At a first meeting in a formal or work situation, a handshake is safe. If the other person leans in for the kisses, go along.

Say Buongiorno until early afternoon, Buonasera from the afternoon on, and Buonanotte only when you say goodnight before sleep. The change from buongiorno to buonasera is around 3 or 4 pm, and it varies from person to person.
Ciao is for friends, family and people of your age, and for children. Salve is a neutral hello between formal and informal. Many Italians say it to a shop assistant or a stranger.
To say goodbye, use Arrivederci. In a formal situation you can say ArrivederLa (goodbye, formal Lei). Ciao also means goodbye between friends.
Customs differ: some people prefer no contact. A handshake and a clear Buongiorno are always fine.

topics.title: Daily rhythm: meal times, opening hours and Sundays
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about daily rhythm in Italy, as of 2026. This is habit, not law: opening hours differ by town, shop and season, and the south and small towns keep a longer midday break than big northern cities. Check the sign on the door or the shop's page.
topics.intro: Italian days follow meals. Breakfast is light, lunch is the main break, and dinner is late. In many towns, shops close for a few hours in the middle of the day and many are closed on Sunday.
topics.question: A che ora mangi di solito? (What time do you usually eat?)
facts: Colazione (breakfast) is small: often a cappuccino and a cornetto, standing at the bar. Many people do not eat a big breakfast.
Pranzo (lunch) is usually between 12:30 and 14:00. For many people it is the main meal, but in big cities office workers often have a quick lunch.

La pausa pranzo is the lunch break. In many towns, shops, small offices and some banks close for lunch, often from about 13:00 to 15:30 or 16:00, then reopen until 19:30 or 20:00. Large shopping centres and big cities often stay open all day.
Cena (dinner) is usually from 20:00 on. Restaurants often open for dinner around 19:30 or 20:00. The kitchen of many places is closed between lunch and dinner.

On Sundays and festivi (public holidays) many small shops, offices and banks are closed. Supermarkets, shopping centres and tourist areas are often open, but not everywhere and not always the whole day.
La domenica a pranzo: Sunday lunch with the family is a strong custom. Restaurants can be full, so book if you want to eat out.
A pharmacy shows a sign for the farmacia di turno (the pharmacy open at night or on Sundays). The list is usually on the door of every pharmacy.

topics.title: The bar: coffee, scontrino, coperto and tips
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about bars and restaurants in Italy, as of 2026. This is habit, not law: prices and rules differ by place and city. Prices are examples and change.
topics.intro: An Italian bar is a cafe: coffee, breakfast, a snack and a drink at the counter. A few small rules make it easy: you often pay first, and drinking at the counter is cheaper than at a table.
topics.question: Dove bevi il caffè di solito? (Where do you usually drink your coffee?)
facts: Un caffè means a small, strong espresso. If you want a milky coffee, say cappuccino, caffè macchiato or caffè latte.
Al banco (at the counter) is cheaper and quicker. At a table (al tavolo) a waiter comes and the price is usually higher. In tourist areas the difference can be large, and the menu shows both prices.

In many busy bars you first go to the cassa (the cash desk), say what you want and pay. You get lo scontrino (the receipt). Then you go to the counter, give the scontrino to the barista and say your order again.
At a small bar the barista may take the money after you drink. Watch what the others do, or ask: Pago prima? (Do I pay first?).

Il coperto is a fixed charge per person in many restaurants (not at the bar counter). It is shown on the menu. It is not a tip. Il servizio (service charge) is a different item and not always present.
Tipping is not expected in Italy. People may leave a little extra in a restaurant after a good meal, or round up the bill, but nobody will be angry if you do not.
Offro io (It is on me) is what you say when you pay for a friend's coffee. Taking turns to pay is normal.

topics.title: The 20 regions of Italy, provinces and comuni
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about the administrative structure of Italy, as of 2026. Official sources: the Constitution (Articles 114 and 116), ISTAT, governo.it. Numbers of provinces and comuni change over time, so check ISTAT for the current figure.
topics.intro: Italy has 20 regioni (regions). Each region has a capoluogo (capital), is divided into provinces, and the provinces into comuni (municipalities). Five regions have a special statute and more self-government.
topics.question: In quale regione vivi o vuoi vivere? (In which region do you live or want to live?)
facts: Italy has 20 regioni, from Valle d'Aosta in the north-west to Sicilia in the south.
Five regions have a regime of special autonomy (regioni a statuto speciale): Valle d'Aosta, Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol, Friuli Venezia Giulia, Sardegna and Sicilia.
Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol has two autonomous provinces, Trento and Bolzano. In Bolzano, German is an official language next to Italian.

A region is divided into province (provinces) and, in big cities, città metropolitane. Roughly 100 provinces and metropolitan cities exist (about 107, to verify). The car plate abbreviation shows the province, for example MI for Milano and RM for Roma.

The smallest unit is the comune. There are close to 8,000 comuni (about 7,900 as of 2025, to verify). Many everyday matters go through the comune: residenza, anagrafe (the register), local taxes and waste collection.
Each region has its own regional government (giunta) and a capital city. The regional capital is not always the biggest city: Trento is the capital of Trentino-Alto Adige, but Bolzano is bigger.
Regions run many services, especially healthcare (the SSN is organised by region), so rules and waiting times can differ between regions.

topics.title: Public holidays: feste nazionali, patron saints and ponti
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about public holidays in Italy, as of 2026. The national list is set by law. Patron saint days are local and differ by comune. Always check the official calendar for the current year.
topics.intro: Italy has twelve national public holidays (giorni festivi). Offices, banks and most shops are closed, and public transport runs on a reduced timetable. Some towns add a day for their patron saint. People also take a ponte (a bridge day) between a holiday and the weekend.
topics.question: Qual è la tua festa preferita? (What is your favourite holiday?)
facts: The national holidays are: 1 gennaio (Capodanno), 6 gennaio (Epifania), Pasqua (Easter Sunday), Lunedì dell'Angelo or Pasquetta (Easter Monday), 25 aprile (Festa della Liberazione), 1 maggio (Festa dei lavoratori), 2 giugno (Festa della Repubblica), 15 agosto (Ferragosto, Assunzione), 1 novembre (Ognissanti), 8 dicembre (Immacolata Concezione), 25 dicembre (Natale) and 26 dicembre (Santo Stefano).
Easter moves every year. Pasqua is on a Sunday in spring, and Pasquetta is the day after. In 2026 Easter Sunday is 5 April (to verify).

Patron saints (il santo patrono) are celebrated locally. For example 7 dicembre Sant'Ambrogio in Milano, 19 settembre San Gennaro in Napoli, 29 giugno Santi Pietro e Paolo in Roma, 24 giugno San Giovanni in Firenze, Genova and Torino, 25 aprile San Marco in Venezia. In the comune concerned, offices and schools are usually closed (to verify per comune and year).
4 novembre (Giorno dell'Unità Nazionale e Giornata delle Forze Armate) is a national commemoration, but it is not a day off (to verify).

I ponti: when a holiday falls on a Tuesday or a Thursday, many people take the Monday or Friday off too and make a long weekend. 25 aprile, 1 maggio and 2 giugno are famous for ponti, and so is the week around 8 dicembre.
Around Ferragosto (15 agosto) many shops and small businesses in cities close for one to three weeks (chiuso per ferie).
If a holiday falls on a Sunday, there is no extra day off in general. Check your contract (CCNL) for details.

topics.title: Food and meals: from colazione to cena
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about meals and food habits in Italy, as of 2026. These are habits, not rules, and they vary by region, family and person. Do not take any of it as the one right way.
topics.intro: Italian meals have a clear order and a clear rhythm. Colazione is light, pranzo and cena can have several courses, and many dishes belong to one region. What is usual in Napoli can be different in Milano.
topics.question: Che cosa mangi a colazione, a pranzo e a cena? (What do you eat for breakfast, lunch and dinner?)
facts: Colazione: coffee or cappuccino with a cornetto, a biscuit or bread with jam. It is often eaten standing at the bar.

Pranzo and cena can have several courses: antipasto (starter), primo (pasta, rice or soup), secondo (meat, fish or eggs), contorno (a side dish of vegetables or salad), then frutta or dolce, and caffè. Nobody eats all of them every day. At home, one or two courses are normal.
Il menu del giorno or menu fisso is a lunch deal at many restaurants on workdays, often with a primo or secondo, a side dish, water and coffee at a fixed price (to verify, differs by place).
L'aperitivo is a drink before dinner, often with small snacks, from about 18:30 to 20:30. In some northern cities, a big aperitivo buffet can almost replace dinner (aperitivo cena).

Pasta is not one thing: every region has its own. Examples: carbonara in Lazio (Roma), orecchiette in Puglia, tortellini in Emilia-Romagna, trofie al pesto in Liguria, pizzoccheri in Lombardia (Valtellina), risotto alla milanese in Lombardia. Pizza is linked to Napoli.

Coffee: after a meal you drink un caffè (an espresso), not a milky coffee. A well-known custom says cappuccino after midday or after a meal is strange, and Italians drink it for breakfast. This is habit, not a rule: nobody will stop you, and bars serve it all day.
Water and wine come with the meal. Acqua naturale (still) or frizzante (sparkling), and vino della casa (house wine) if you want. Meals are slow: waiters do not bring the bill until you ask.

topics.title: Festivals: feste, sagre and patron saints
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about festivals in Italy, as of 2026. Dates of many festivals move each year, and local feasts differ by comune. Check the local programme before you travel.
topics.intro: Italy has festivals all year: big historical events, religious feasts and small village sagre. Many are tied to a place, a saint or a food.
topics.question: Quale festa vuoi vedere in Italia? (Which festival do you want to see in Italy?)
facts: Carnevale is in February or early March, before Lent, and the date changes each year. The Carnevale di Venezia is famous for masks and costumes. The Carnevale di Viareggio is known for its big floats of papier-mache that parade along the sea front.
Pasqua (Easter) has processions in Holy Week in many places, and families eat together on Easter Sunday and Pasquetta, often outdoors.
Il Palio di Siena is a horse race in the main square, Piazza del Campo, between the contrade (districts of the city). It is held twice a year, on 2 July and 16 August (to verify).
Ferragosto, 15 August, is the middle of the summer holiday. Many people go to the sea or the mountains, and cities are quiet.
La Festa della Repubblica, 2 June, remembers the referendum of 1946. There is an official parade in Roma.
Natale is on 25 December, and la Befana comes on 6 January: according to tradition, a kind old woman brings sweets to children, and coal-shaped sweets to those who were naughty.

A sagra is a local village festival with a food as the star, for example the sagra della porchetta or the sagra del tartufo. Typical in late summer and autumn. Patron saint feasts such as San Gennaro (19 September, Napoli) and Sant'Ambrogio (7 December, Milano) bring processions, fairs and local sweets.

topics.title: Raccolta differenziata: sorting your rubbish
topics.sourceNote: General orientation about household waste in Italy, as of 2026, not legal advice. The categories are similar everywhere, but the bin colours, the collection days and the rules are set by each Comune (town hall) and its waste company, so they differ from town to town. Check the ecocalendario on your Comune's website.
topics.intro: In Italy you sort your rubbish at home (la raccolta differenziata). The categories are almost the same everywhere, but the colours, the bags and the collection days change from Comune to Comune. Ask at the Comune or look at the ecocalendario.
topics.question: Come differenzi i rifiuti nel tuo paese? (How do you sort rubbish in your country?)
facts: Umido or organico: food scraps, coffee grounds, tea bags, peelings. Many towns give you a small kitchen bin and compostable bags (sacchetti compostabili). Plastic bags do not go in.
Carta e cartone: paper, newspapers, cardboard boxes. Flatten the boxes first. Greasy pizza boxes often go in the umido or the secco: check your Comune.
Plastica e lattine: plastic bottles, packaging, tins and cans. In many places metal and plastic go together, in others they are separate.
Vetro: bottles and jars, without lids. Drinking glasses, ceramics and mirrors usually do not go in.
Secco or indifferenziato: everything that cannot be recycled. Some towns use a special bag, a key card or fixed days for it.

Bulky items (ingombranti), batteries, electronics, oil and chemicals go to the isola ecologica (recycling centre), or you can book a free collection of ingombranti with your waste company. Rules, hours and costs depend on your Comune.

topics.intro: In Italy some offices let you walk in and take a number, and others only see you with an appointment. Health visits go through the CUP, and for the permesso di soggiorno there is an online portal. Always check the office's own website first.
topics.question: Come prenoti un appuntamento nel tuo paese? (How do you book an appointment in your country?)
facts: Many offices (Comune, ASL, INPS, Agenzia delle Entrate) let you book online or by phone. Others work with a numero da ritirare: at the entrance you take a ticket from the eliminacode machine and wait until your number is called at a sportello (counter).

For health visits and tests with a specialist you book through the CUP (Centro Unico di Prenotazione): online, by phone, at the pharmacy or at the ASL. You usually need the impegnativa (the doctor's prescription) and your tessera sanitaria.

For the permesso di soggiorno you often first send a kit at the post office, then you get an appointment letter from the Questura. Many things are also handled through the Questura's online portal (to verify for your city).

Many online services ask for SPID or CIE (digital identity) to log in. Not everyone has one. At many offices you can ask a patronato (a free help desk) for support. To verify which service you can use as a foreign resident.
A PEC (posta elettronica certificata) is a certified email address that counts like a registered letter. Companies and offices use it; for private people it is not always needed.
On the day arrive ten minutes early with the confirmation, a document and all your papers. If you cannot come, cancel or move the appointment so that someone else can use it.

topics.sourceNote: General orientation, as of 2026, not legal advice. The rules for the cambio di residenza are national, but offices and forms differ by Comune. The documents depend on whether you are an EU citizen or not. Ask your Comune's Anagrafe or the official website for what applies to you.
topics.intro: In Italy you register where you live at the Anagrafe of your Comune. That is your residenza. Many other things depend on it: the medico di base, the carta d'identità, often a bank account or a lease.
topics.question: Come ti registri quando cambi città nel tuo paese? (How do you register when you move in your country?)
facts: The Anagrafe is the register office of the Comune. When you move into a flat, you ask for the iscrizione anagrafica or the cambio di residenza there.
The rule is that you ask within 20 days of the move. This is general orientation (to verify for your case). You can often do it online, by registered mail, by PEC or at the office.

After your request the vigili urbani (local police) may come to your flat to check that you really live there. Then the Comune confirms the registration. The check can take some time, so keep your name on the doorbell.

You usually need an identity document, the address, and a document that shows your right to live there: lease, ownership deed or a declaration by the owner. Non-EU citizens also need a valid permesso di soggiorno (to verify).
EU citizens and non-EU citizens have different rules and documents, for example for stays over three months or the attestazione di soggiorno. To verify with your Comune.

Afterwards you can ask for the certificato di residenza, the stato di famiglia (everyone living in your household) and the carta d'identità. Many certificates can be requested online or at the office; some have a small fee.

Italy's public health service (Servizio Sanitario Nazionale, SSN) is organised by the regions, so names (ASL, AST, ASP), forms and ticket amounts differ. For foreign residents, who may register and on what terms depends on the status: ask your local ASL.
topics.intro: Italy has a public health service, the SSN. Residents usually register with their local ASL, get a tessera sanitaria and choose a medico di base (family doctor). For most things you go through the medico di base first.
topics.question: Come funziona la sanità nel tuo paese? (How does health care work in your country?)
facts: The SSN is run by the regions through local health authorities (ASL; in some regions called AST or ASP). You register at your ASL, usually with your residenza or a similar document. The rules for foreign residents depend on your status (to verify with the ASL).
The tessera sanitaria is your health card. You show it for visits, tests and at the pharmacy.

You choose a medico di base (also called medico di famiglia) from a list at the ASL. This is the scelta del medico. The doctor writes the ricetta (prescription) and the impegnativa (referral) for specialist visits and tests.
For specialists and tests you book through the CUP with the impegnativa. Often you pay a ticket (a contribution), and the amount depends on the service and on your region and income (to verify).

In an emergency call 118 (ambulance) or 112 (single European emergency number) or go to the pronto soccorso (emergency room). At night and at weekends the guardia medica takes less urgent cases when your doctor is not available.
The farmacia is open to everyone for advice and medicine. Medicine with a ricetta is often cheaper or free, depending on the case. Pharmacies on duty (di turno) stay open at night.

topics.intro: Flats for rent in Italy are advertised as "affittasi". The contract usually has a fixed length, it is registered with the tax office, and you pay a deposit and monthly costs. Read everything before you sign.
topics.question: Com'è affittare una casa nel tuo paese? (What is renting a flat like in your country?)
facts: The usual free-market contract is a 4+4: four years, then automatically four more years. The canone concordato (agreed rent) contract is a 3+2: three years, then two. It follows local rent agreements and can have tax advantages (to verify).
The caparra or deposito cauzionale is a deposit, often up to three months' rent. It must be returned at the end if the flat is in good condition (to verify the exact limits).

Spese condominiali are the building costs (cleaning, lift, heating if shared). The contract says what you pay. Utenze (luce, gas, water, internet) are normally in your name: you ask for a new account or a voltura (change of name).

The contract must be registered with the Agenzia delle Entrate within 30 days. Normally the owner does this. You can choose the cedolare secca (a flat tax for the owner) instead of the normal registration costs (to verify).
Many people use an agenzia immobiliare. The agency fee (provvigione) is often paid by the tenant, usually one to two months' rent plus VAT, but this varies (to verify).
To register your residenza at the new address you need the contract, so check with the landlord that you are allowed to register there.

topics.sourceNote: General orientation, as of 2026, not legal advice. Ages and names are the national pattern; exact rules, enrolment dates and costs change and differ by school and region. Check the Ministry of Education and Merit (MIM) and the school's own website.
topics.intro: School in Italy is organised in stages. Education is compulsory from 6 to 16 years, and many children start earlier at the scuola dell'infanzia. You enrol your child online, in a period set by the ministry each year.
topics.question: Com'è la scuola nel tuo paese? (What is school like in your country?)
facts: Scuola dell'infanzia (kindergarten), ages 3 to 6, is not compulsory. Scuola primaria (elementary), ages 6 to 11, five years.
Scuola secondaria di primo grado (middle school), ages 11 to 14, three years, ends with an exam. After it children choose a school for the next stage (to verify details).
Scuola secondaria di secondo grado, ages 14 to 19: licei (classical, scientific, languages and others), istituti tecnici and istituti professionali. It ends with the esame di maturità.
Compulsory schooling (obbligo scolastico) runs from age 6 to 16, and training or education is expected until 18 (to verify).
You enrol online (iscrizione online) on the ministry's platform in a period in winter, usually January (to verify the dates each year). With SPID or CIE you can log in; the school can help.

Public schools are free to attend, but you may pay for the mensa (school lunch), transport and extra activities, and often for books (libri), depending on the region and school (to verify). Schools also help children who are new to Italian.

facts: The Centro per l'impiego (public employment office) helps you register as a job seeker and look for offers. The details of the services differ by region (to verify).
Your CV is the curriculum (CV). The Europass format is common, but a clear, short CV in Italian is enough. Add a short lettera di presentazione when you apply.
Agenzie per il lavoro (employment agencies) place people with companies, often with temporary contracts (somministrazione). They do not charge the worker a fee.

Contract types: tempo indeterminato (permanent), tempo determinato (fixed-term), apprendistato (training with a contract), lavoro stagionale (seasonal). The contract says the hours, the pay and the CCNL that applies.

At the start there is often a periodo di prova (trial period), the length depends on the CCNL and the role. Each month you receive a busta paga (payslip) that shows gross pay, contributions and taxes: check it.

Lavoro nero (undeclared work) means no contributions, no protection, and risk for you, including problems with the permesso di soggiorno. Non-EU citizens need a valid permesso di soggiorno that allows work (permesso per lavoro) to work legally (to verify your case).

topics.title: Languages and dialects of Italy
topics.sourceNote: General orientation based on law 482/1999 on the protection of historical linguistic minorities and the special statutes of Valle d'Aosta and Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol, as of 2026. Rules for schools and offices differ by region, so ask locally.
topics.intro: Italian is the official language of the whole country, but people speak much more than standard Italian. There are dialects in every region and several recognised minority languages. For a learner this means that the Italian you hear on the street can sound different from the Italian in your course book.
topics.question: Che lingua o dialetto si parla nella tua zona? (Which language or dialect is spoken where you live?)
facts: Standard Italian is based on the Tuscan of Florence and is used in school, in the media and in offices all over the country.
Dialetti are not 'bad Italian'. Many of them are separate Romance varieties with their own history, such as Neapolitan, Venetian, Sicilian or Milanese. Many Italians speak both a dialect and Italian.
Law 482/1999 recognises 12 historical minority languages. They include Sardinian, Friulian, Ladin, German, French, Slovene, Albanian, Catalan, Greek, Croatian, Franco-Provençal and Occitan.

French has a special status in Valle d'Aosta, and German in the province of Bolzano (Alto Adige/Südtirol). There, schools, signs and offices can work in two languages, with rules that are set locally.
Catalan is spoken in Alghero in Sardinia. Greek is spoken in some villages in Calabria and Puglia. Albanian is spoken in communities in the south that have lived there for centuries.
Regional accents differ clearly. A Tuscan, a Roman, a Milanese and a Neapolitan speaker all use Italian, but the sounds, the rhythm and some words are different. A learner will meet all of them.

topics.intro: If you want to leave your job, there are rules for the notice and for how the resignation must be sent. If the employer ends the job, that is a licenziamento. In both cases you should check what you still receive: the last pay, the TFR and possible unemployment benefit.

You may have a short time to revoke the resignation after you send it (often 7 days, to verify).
The TFR (trattamento di fine rapporto) is a severance amount that is built up over the years and paid when the job ends. It is shown on your final payslip or paid shortly after.

NASpI is the unemployment benefit. In general it is for people who lose their job involuntarily and who have enough contributions, but there are exceptions, such as dismissal or resignation for a good reason (giusta causa). Conditions and amounts change (to verify).
In case of licenziamento the employer must give a written reason. If you think it is unfair, ask a union or a labour lawyer soon, because there are short deadlines (to verify).

Which office handles what can differ by region and by comune, so check the official page of your comune or region. General orientation, not legal advice.
topics.intro: Italy is one Republic made of comuni, province, città metropolitane, regioni and the State. Each level has its own tasks. Knowing which level handles what tells you where to go for a certificate, a health appointment or a permit.
topics.question: Come è organizzato il territorio nel tuo Paese? (How is the territory organised in your country?)
facts: Article 114 of the Constitution says that the Republic is made up of the comuni, the province, the città metropolitane, the regioni and the State. Since the constitutional reform of 2001 (Titolo V) the regions and local bodies have more powers than before.

Italy has 20 regioni. Five of them have a special statute (statuto speciale) with extra autonomy: Valle d'Aosta, Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Sardegna and Sicilia. Trentino-Alto Adige is in practice made of two autonomous provinces, Trento and Bolzano. The other 15 are regioni a statuto ordinario.

Article 117 divides the powers. The State has exclusive power over matters such as foreign affairs, immigration, citizenship, defence and the courts. Some matters are shared (concurrent), for example health protection and some parts of education, and everything not listed goes to the regions. The wording of the list is long, so use the official text.

There are about 100 provincial-level bodies, including 14 città metropolitane (such as Roma, Milano, Napoli and Torino), as of 2026 (to verify). The province looks after things like secondary-school buildings and provincial roads. The prefetto, who represents the State in each province, runs the Prefettura.

Italy has about 7,900 comuni (ISTAT, 2025, to verify), led by a sindaco who is elected directly. The comune keeps the Anagrafe (residence, certificates, carta d'identità), the stato civile, local police, waste and local taxes.

In practice: the Comune handles anagrafe and local services, the Regione organises the health service (the Servizio sanitario nazionale is run regionally through the ASL, so rules like ticket and waiting lists differ), and the State handles police and immigration through the Questura and the Prefettura (to verify the details for your case).

topics.intro: Almost every step in Italian working life asks for a codice fiscale. Contributions go to INPS (pensions, unemployment, family benefits) and to INAIL (accidents at work). Knowing the three names helps you read a busta paga and talk to an office.
topics.question: Come funziona la previdenza sociale nel tuo Paese? (How does social insurance work in your country?)
facts: The codice fiscale is a 16-character code that identifies you for tax and public services. The Agenzia delle Entrate issues it, also to foreigners (at an office or, from abroad, through the consulate, to verify). You need it for a work contract, a bank account, a rental contract and registration with the health service.

The tessera sanitaria is the health card, and it carries your codice fiscale. It is issued after you register with the Servizio sanitario nazionale at the ASL (see the topic on public health). The codice fiscale is not the same as the partita IVA.

The partita IVA is an 11-digit number for self-employed people and businesses, opened at the Agenzia delle Entrate. Many freelancers use the regime forfettario with a flat tax under a turnover limit (the limit and rate are to verify, as of 2026). A freelancer pays contributions to INPS (Gestione separata or a category fund such as artigiani and commercianti).

INPS (Istituto nazionale della previdenza sociale) pays pensions, unemployment benefit (NASpI), sickness and maternity allowances and the assegno unico per i figli. Employer and employee both pay contributions, and the share is shown on the busta paga (about a third of gross pay in total for an employee, with the employer paying the larger part, to verify).

INAIL (Istituto nazionale per l'assicurazione contro gli infortuni sul lavoro) insures workers against accidents at work and occupational diseases. The employer pays INAIL, not the worker. After an accident you report it to the employer and the doctor sends the certificate to INAIL.

For the pension, the ordinary old-age pension needs a minimum age (67 years in 2026, to verify) and at least 20 years of contributions (to verify). Your estratto conto contributivo shows your contributions year by year and you can see it in the My INPS area with SPID or CIE. A patronato (such as INCA, INAS, ITAL, ACLI) helps for free with these forms.

topics.sourceNote: Costituzione italiana (art. 48, 56, 57, 75, 138), the electoral law known as Rosatellum (legge 165/2017), the 2020 and 2021 constitutional changes, interno.gov.it, as of 2026 (to verify the numbers). topics.intro: Italy is a parliamentary republic. Citizens vote for the Parliament, for the European Parliament and in local elections, and they can vote in referendums. Knowing the basic rules helps you follow the news and understand who can vote and who cannot.
topics.question: Chi può votare nel tuo Paese? (Who can vote in your country?)
facts: The Parliament has two chambers with equal powers (bicameralismo perfetto): the Camera dei deputati and the Senato della Repubblica. Since the 2022 election, after the reform confirmed by referendum in 2020, there are 400 deputies and 200 elected senators (before: 630 and 315). There are also a few senators for life (to verify).

Everyone aged 18 or older can vote for both chambers. Until a constitutional change in 2021 (to verify) the Senate vote began at 25. To be elected, you must be 25 for the Camera and 40 for the Senate (to verify).

The current electoral law, called Rosatellum (2017), is a mixed system: about one third of seats are won in single-member constituencies (the candidate with most votes wins) and about two thirds are assigned proportionally, with a threshold of 3% for lists (the exact shares are to verify). A small number of seats are for Italians living abroad, who can vote by post.

The last general election was on 25 September 2022. The Government needs the confidence (fiducia) of both chambers. The President of the Republic is elected by Parliament together with regional delegates, not directly by citizens.

Referendums: the abrogative referendum (art. 75) can repeal a law, and it is valid only if more than half of the voters take part. The constitutional referendum (art. 138) has no quorum. In the comunali the sindaco is elected directly by the citizens.

Non-citizens cannot vote in national elections or national referendums. Citizens of other EU countries who live in Italy can vote and stand in the comunali and in the European elections, after registering on the electoral roll (to verify). You get the tessera elettorale from the Ufficio elettorale of your comune, and you bring it with an ID to the polling station.

topics.title: Italian emigration and the Italian diaspora
topics.sourceNote: General historical overview written neutrally. Figures are rounded and come from ISTAT, the Fondazione Migrantes (Rapporto Italiani nel Mondo) and the Ministero degli Affari Esteri, as of 2026 (to verify). Historians and governments assess these events differently, and this page does not take a side. Citizenship rules change, so ask the official source.
topics.intro: Between the unification and the 1970s millions of Italians left their country. Today Italy is mainly a destination, and many people in Argentina, Brazil, the USA and elsewhere have Italian roots. This history explains why many Italian families live on several continents.
topics.question: C'è emigrazione nella storia del tuo Paese? (Is there emigration in your country's history?)
facts: From about 1876, when the first official statistics begin, until about 1976 around 27 million people left Italy (figure rounded, to verify). The first big wave came mostly from the north-east, later from the south, and the peak years were just before World War I.

The main destinations before 1945 were the Americas: Argentina, Brazil and the USA, then also Uruguay, Venezuela and Canada. Many moved only for some years, and many came back. Ellis Island in New York was the main entry point to the USA from 1892.

After World War II the direction changed towards Europe: Switzerland, Germany, Belgium and France. In 1946 Italy and Belgium signed an agreement on work in the mines. The accident at Marcinelle on 8 August 1956 killed 262 miners, more than half of them Italians (to verify). Each year Italy remembers Italian workers abroad on 8 August (to verify).

From the 1970s Italy had more arrivals than departures. Immigration grew in the 1990s, for example after the arrival of ships from Albania in 1991. As of 2026 about 5 million foreign citizens live in Italy (ISTAT, to verify).

The AIRE (Anagrafe degli Italiani Residenti all'Estero) is the register of Italian citizens who live abroad. It exists since 1988 and counts about 6 million people today (Ministero dell'Interno, to verify). Citizens abroad can vote, by post, for the Parliament and have seats reserved for them.

Italian citizenship by descent (ius sanguinis) is the reason why many descendants abroad have a passport. The rules were restricted in 2025 and now depend on a parent or grandparent born in Italy, with further conditions (to verify). Today young Italians still move abroad for work, and the topic is discussed in different ways by different people.

topics.title: From the Republic of 1946 to today
topics.sourceNote: General historical overview written neutrally. Dates follow standard reference works and official sites (quirinale.it, governo.it, camera.it), as of 2026 (to verify the figures). Historians judge some of these events differently, and this page does not take a side on party questions.
topics.intro: The Italian Republic was born on 2 June 1946 after fascism and the war. A few dates explain the national holidays, the Constitution and why Italy is a founder of the European Community. They also help you follow conversations about the 25 aprile and the 2 giugno.
topics.question: Quali date della storia del tuo Paese sono giorni di festa? (Which dates in your country's history are holidays?)
facts: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861. Rome became the capital in 1871. In 1922 (28 October, the March on Rome) Mussolini took power, and in the years that followed fascism ended the democratic freedoms. In 1938 the racial laws were passed (to verify the exact dates).

Italy entered World War II on 10 June 1940. On 25 July 1943 Mussolini was removed, and on 8 September 1943 the armistice was announced. The country was then divided between the German occupation and the Allies, and the Resistenza (partisans, with the CLN) fought against the occupation and the fascist republic of Salò.

25 April 1945 is the Festa della Liberazione, a national holiday since 1949 (to verify). It marks the liberation of the northern cities. Women voted in a general vote for the first time on 2 June 1946: the right to vote had been given by decree in 1945 and local elections took place in March 1946.

On 2 June 1946 Italians chose between monarchy and republic in a referendum: about 54% voted for the Republic (rounded, to verify). On the same day they elected the Assemblea Costituente, which wrote the Constitution. Enrico De Nicola became the first provisional head of state, and Alcide De Gasperi led the first governments.

In the Cold War Italy joined NATO in 1949 and was one of the six founding states of the European Economic Community with the Treaty of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957. The years from about 1958 to 1963 are called the boom economico. The late 1960s to the 1980s were marked by political violence (the anni di piombo, to verify).

In 1992-1994 the Tangentopoli investigations (Mani pulite) changed the party system. Euro banknotes and coins arrived on 1 January 2002 and the lira stopped being legal tender at the end of February 2002 (to verify). Today 2 June is the Festa della Repubblica.

topics.title: The Constitution of 1948 and the Constitutional Court
topics.sourceNote: Costituzione della Repubblica italiana (text on quirinale.it and normattiva.it), art. 1-12, 83-91, 104, 134-139, as of 2026. Quoted wording of articles is given from memory of the official text and is to verify. This is general orientation, not legal advice.
topics.intro: The Constitution is the basic law of the Republic. It sets the principles, the rights and the organs of the State, and the Corte costituzionale checks that ordinary laws respect it. These words appear often in the news and in civic exams.
topics.question: Quali diritti garantisce la Costituzione del tuo Paese? (Which rights does your country's constitution guarantee?)
facts: The Constitution was approved by the Assemblea Costituente on 22 December 1947, promulgated on 27 December 1947 and entered into force on 1 January 1948. It has 139 articles plus transitional and final provisions (to verify). Articles 1 to 12 are the fundamental principles.

Article 1 begins: 'L'Italia è una Repubblica democratica, fondata sul lavoro.' It adds that sovereignty belongs to the people, who use it in the forms and limits of the Constitution. Article 3 says that all citizens have equal social dignity and are equal before the law, without distinction of sex, race, language, religion, political opinion or personal and social conditions (to verify the exact wording).

Article 6 protects linguistic minorities (such as German speakers in Alto Adige, Slovene speakers and French speakers in Valle d'Aosta). Article 7 says that the State and the Catholic Church are independent and sovereign in their own order, and article 8 says that all religious confessions are equally free (to verify). Article 12 sets the tricolour flag.

The President of the Republic is head of state and guarantee of the Constitution, elected by Parliament in joint session with regional delegates for seven years (art. 83-91). The Consiglio superiore della magistratura (CSM, art. 104) governs the judiciary and is chaired by the President of the Republic.

The Corte costituzionale (art. 134-137) has 15 judges: five appointed by the President of the Republic, five elected by Parliament in joint session and five chosen by the highest courts. They serve nine years (to verify). The Court decides whether a law is constitutional, settles conflicts between State bodies and between State and regions, and admits referendums.

The Constitution can be revised only with a special procedure (art. 138), with two readings in each chamber and, if requested, a referendum. It is the reference for everything from the right to strike to the right to health (art. 32). To read it in full, use the official text, not a summary.

topics.sourceNote: Costituzione (art. 36, 39, 40), Statuto dei lavoratori (legge 300/1970), d.lgs. 66/2003 on working time, the websites of CGIL, CISL, UIL, USB, the Ministero del Lavoro and the Ispettorato nazionale del lavoro, as of 2026 (figures to verify). General orientation, not legal advice: for your own contract ask a union, a patronato or the Ispettorato del lavoro.
topics.intro: In Italy many basic terms of a job, such as pay levels, hours and holidays, come from a national collective agreement (CCNL), negotiated by unions and employers. Knowing the unions and the main rights helps you read your contract and your busta paga.
topics.question: Che cosa fa un sindacato nel tuo Paese? (What does a union do in your country?)
facts: The best-known confederations are the CGIL, the CISL and the UIL. There are also smaller ones such as USB. Joining is voluntary (art. 39 of the Constitution): you usually sign a delega and a small share of pay goes to the union (to verify).

The Statuto dei lavoratori (legge 20 maggio 1970, n. 300) protects freedom of opinion at work, union activity in the workplace and limits on controls over workers. Some of its rules, for example on dismissal, changed with later reforms (to verify).

A CCNL (contratto collettivo nazionale di lavoro) is negotiated for a sector, for example commercio, metalmeccanici or edilizia. It sets minimum pay by level (livello), weekly hours, holidays, sick pay, notice periods and other terms. Italy has no single statutory minimum wage, so the CCNL is the reference (to verify). Your contract and busta paga name the CCNL that applies.

Standard rules (d.lgs. 66/2003, to verify): normal working time is 40 hours per week, at least 4 weeks of paid annual leave (ferie), a daily rest period and a weekly rest day. In case of illness (malattia) the doctor sends a certificate with a protocol number to INPS and you tell your employer; the pay depends on the CCNL.

In a workplace, workers can be represented by the RSA or the RSU (rappresentanza sindacale unitaria, elected by all workers). Article 40 of the Constitution says that the right to strike is exercised within the laws that regulate it. In essential public services special rules apply (law 146/1990, to verify).

If there is a problem (unpaid wages, a wrong level, an unfair dismissal), a union or a patronato can help for free or at low cost. A vertenza usually starts with a request to the employer, then a conciliazione, the Ispettorato territoriale del lavoro and, if needed, the giudice del lavoro. Deadlines are short, so ask quickly.
